questions.q: What does the what-if parameter in this project need to do?
options: Feed a calculated field so that adjusting the parameter causes the numbers to visibly and correctly recompute
Simply display a static label with no effect on the data
Only change the dashboard's color scheme
Replace the need for any calculated fields entirely
questions.explain: A what-if parameter (like a Discount Cap or Profit Target) must drive a real calculation — dragging it should change a computed value like Simulated Profit, verifiably and correctly.

questions.q: Why does the rubric specifically require Compute Using to be deliberately configured on the table calculation, rather than left on Tableau's default?
options: Because the default addressing/partitioning may not match the actual intent (e.g., ranking sub-categories within each region specifically), and leaving it on default risks a silently wrong result
Because Compute Using only affects visual formatting, not the underlying numbers
Because Tableau requires Compute Using to be set before a workbook can be published
Because table calculations are disabled by default until configured
questions.explain: Compute Using controls how a table calculation is scoped (e.g., ranking within region vs. across the whole table) — leaving it on default can silently produce a technically-working but conceptually wrong result.

questions.q: What is a 'navigation action' in the context of this project's dashboard actions?
options: A dashboard action, usually a button, that takes the viewer to another dashboard or sheet
A filter that removes navigation menus from the published view
A parameter that controls the what-if scenario
An action that only works on Tableau Public, not Server or Cloud
questions.explain: Navigation actions let a viewer move between connected dashboards or sheets, which is part of what makes a multi-sheet project read as one connected experience rather than isolated screens.

questions.q: What tool does the lesson specify for building a mobile or tablet layout of the dashboard?
options: Tableau's Device Designer
A separate, entirely new workbook built from scratch
Tableau Public's mobile export feature
The Performance Recorder
questions.explain: Device Designer is Tableau's built-in tool for creating layout variants of a dashboard specific to phone or tablet screens, and the rubric requires a genuinely usable version, not just a shrunk desktop layout.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what makes this project deliberately harder than Projects 1 and 2?
options: It's meant to combine every major Tableau capability from the course — parameters, LOD expressions, table calculations, and navigation — into one working, explainable whole
It uses a completely different, unfamiliar dataset
It requires no calculated fields at all, unlike the earlier projects
It must be built without using any dashboard actions
questions.explain: Project 3 is explicitly designed as the capstone-level piece that proves the ability to combine multiple advanced Tableau capabilities into one cohesive, demoable deliverable — exactly what a real BI role expects on day one.
